title: Two American women attempt to smuggle US$1 million worth of cannabis into Tokyo for a free trip to Japan
description: Suspect says she wanted to see Japan, but this was not the way to go about it.  One of the first things any visitor to Japan should know is that the country takes a hard stance against drugs – so much so that even common prescription drugs from overseas face stricter restrictions on these shores. […]
content:
Suspect says she wanted to see Japan, but this was not the way to go about it. 

One of the first things any visitor to Japan should know is that the country takes a hard stance against drugs – so much so that even common prescription drugs from overseas face stricter restrictions on these shores.

So if someone offers you a free trip to Japan on the proviso that you bring cannabis into the country, you’d be best off saying no, because chances are you won’t get in to see the country and you may never be allowed in ever again.

That’s the hard reality now being faced by two U.S. citizens who didn’t say no, and the irony is that the reason given for taking the job was a desire to see Japan. Neither of them made it past Haneda Airport, though, because they were stopped by customs officials after arriving on a flight from New York on 5 September, and after their luggage was inspected, 35 bags of dried cannabis were found hidden inside two suitcases.

The haul weighed in at around 30 kilograms (66 pounds), with an estimated street value of around 150 million yen (about US$1 million).

▼ This news report shows the drugs that were seized.

After their arrest, one of the suspects, a 25-year-old, admitted to the allegations of smuggling and said she had heard that working as a drug courier meant her airfare and accommodation would be covered. She also said she was attracted by the opportunity to visit Japan. The second suspect has denied the allegations.

Despite the desire to see Japan, the only thing the two suspects will now be seeing is the justice system firsthand. Under Japanese law, suspects can be held without charge for up to 23 days, and with a prevailing guilty-until-proven innocent mindset within the justice system, the conviction rate among those charged is incredibly high, at around 99 percent.

▼ Once these are on, there’s a high chance of a conviction.

Importing cannabis carries a maximum sentence of seven years in prison, while importing it for profit carries a maximum of 10 years’ imprisonment and potentially a fine of up to 3 million yen (about $19,500).

Foreign nationals convicted of drug offences can be denied entry to Japan with no specified period of exclusion. That means there isn’t a statutory period after which the prohibition automatically expires, so you could be denied entry for decades afterwards.

You don’t have to be carrying a large haul of drugs either, as Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare explicitly states that importing cannabis and cannabis resin is prohibited.

So if you’ve ever toyed with the idea of bringing cannabis into Japan, don’t. Not only will you face severe penalties, you run the chance of being caught up in Japan’s legal system, which doesn’t play by the same rules as those abroad. Plus, you may not be allowed into the country in future, which is something that even celebrities like Paris Hilton, the Rolling Stones and Paul McCartney have experienced, due to previous drug convictions outside the country.

Sources: Nikkei, NTV News, Yahoo! Japan News

title: TeamLab is building a new Tokyo museum, and it’s the digital art group’s biggest ever
description: As TeamLab’s fame continues to grow, so too does the size of its art museums. At the time of its founding in 2001, TeamLab didn’t attract all that much attention. Sure, the Japanese creative group’s professed purpose of mixing art, science, and technology sounded conceptually cool, but when it comes to actual execution, that’s a […]
content:
As TeamLab’s fame continues to grow, so too does the size of its art museums.

At the time of its founding in 2001, TeamLab didn’t attract all that much attention. Sure, the Japanese creative group’s professed purpose of mixing art, science, and technology sounded conceptually cool, but when it comes to actual execution, that’s a combination that no small number of art collectives have stumbled over.

Fast-forward to a quarter-century later, though, and TeamLab has become world-famous for the distinct way in which it creates ethereally enchanting spaces through the skillful use of digital effects to create interplays of light, shadow, and color. With TeamLab’s fanbase continuing to grow and its art installations often considered must-visit attractions for travelers in Japan, the group is ready to take its next step and has announced that a brand-new TeamLab museum will be opening in Tokyo.

TeamLab currently has two locations in Tokyo, with the above-pictured TeamLab Borderless having opened in the Azabudai neighborhood in 2024. While it’s drawn more than four million visitors since then, TeamLab Borderless is a reduced-size version of the facility of the same name that used to be located inside the now-closed Palette Town entertainment complex in Tokyo’s Odaiba neighborhood on an island in Tokyo Bay.

For its new museum, tentatively named TeamLab Tokyo, TeamLab will be headed back to Tokyo Bay, this time to the Ariake district adjacent to Odaiba. TeamLab Tokyo is slated to be a 33,000-square-meter (322,917-square-foot) facility, significantly larger than either TeamLab Borderless or Team Lab Planets in Tokyo’s Toyosu area. As a matter of fact, TeamLab Tokyo will be the largest TeamLab facility the group has ever built, and in addition to digital art installations will have a plaza, open spaces with greenery, and a cafe, as shown in the concept image at the top of this article.

▼ TeamLab Planets

Demand for TeamLab Tokyo tickets is sure to be high, but the rush to reserve them is yet to start, as the museum is projected to open in 2032. As of this time, TeamLab hasn’t announced any plans to close either of its current Tokyo facilities, though that could change between now and when the TeamLab Tokyo opens its doors.

Source: PR Times, Bijutsu Techo

title: Tokyo’s Shibuya puts up new posters asking visitors to use recycle boxes properly
description: Campaign is neighborhood’s latest attempt to keep litter and overtourism in check. It wasn’t all that long ago that Tokyo’s Shibuya neighborhood was pretty firmly in the “only if you have spare time” section of most tourists’ Japan travel plans. Sure, Shibuya always had shops, restaurants, bars, and clubs, but the common attitude was that […]
content:
Campaign is neighborhood’s latest attempt to keep litter and overtourism in check.

It wasn’t all that long ago that Tokyo’s Shibuya neighborhood was pretty firmly in the “only if you have spare time” section of most tourists’ Japan travel plans. Sure, Shibuya always had shops, restaurants, bars, and clubs, but the common attitude was that there were better ones to be found in Harajuku, Ginza, Shinjuku, or Roppongi, especially for those visiting from abroad.

Nowadays, though, Shibuya has become a must-see part of Tokyo for many visitors from overseas who want to experience crossing the now-world-famous Shibuya Scramble intersection, snap a photo with the statue of faithful dog Hachiko, check out the exclusive merch at the Shibuya Pokémon Center, and otherwise bask in the multitude of backdrops for eye-catching selfies for social media.

Along with increased tourist numbers, though, Shibuya has also been seeing increased levels of litter, which is leading to a new plea to help keep the neighborhood clean.

On September 1, Shibuya Ward and the Japan Soft Drink Association launched a joint public awareness campaign reminding everyone not only to use the recycling containers placed next to vending machines, but to use them properly. Posters, with both English and Japanese-text versions, make it clear that the recycling containers are for empty drink containers only, specifically PET (plastic) bottles, glass bottles, and cans.

Anything else needs to be disposed of elsewhere, and the posters emphasize four items in particular. While the recycling boxes are for empty drink containers, they’re not for empty plastic cups of the kind you’d get with a Starbucks Frappuccino or convenience store smoothie. Because of their size and shape, cups of this type can block the receptacle’s opening, preventing others from being able to use it as intended. Plastic bags also aren’t supposed to go in the recycling box, nor are mobile batteries or cigarette butts. The poster also makes a special point of explaining, to anyone thinking they’ve found a clever loophole, that putting cigarette butts or other trash inside a plastic bottle and then putting that bottle inside the box is also not allowed.

▼ The Japanese-text version of the poster. It’s strange that the illustration shows a crushed can, and it’s best not to distort their shape, so that they’ll slide more easily into the recycling box’s opening.

The physical printed poster is being displayed at a half-dozen public smoking areas in Shibuya, and notices are also being displayed on the signage system inside and outside Shibuya’s Miyashita Park entertainment complex.

In addition, bilingual English/Japanese reminder videos will play in the area around Shibuya Station, and the campaign’s organizers say they plan to add Chinese and Korean-language materials to spread the word as well.

▼ A still from the video message

The move follows a recent amendment to Shibuya’s local ordinances, which now require more public trash cans, plus new fines for littering that went into effect this summer.

Though it’s unfortunate that part of the price of less litter appears to be putting up a bunch of extra cautionary notices, hopefully the campaign will help instill a sense of how important it is to dispose of waste in its proper place, and maybe some day doing so really will become something visitors do as a common-sense matter of course.

title: Don Quijote ear cleaner sucks, and was criticised by customers, but is the new version any better?
description: Find out if the new ear cleaner sucks more than the old one. A lot of companies have their own private brands in Japan, with one being the zany, buy-anything-and-everything-in-one-place retail chain Don Quijote. Called Jonetsu Kakaku (literally “Passion Price”), this range of goods focuses on fun goods that are affordable and convenient to use, […]
content:
Find out if the new ear cleaner sucks more than the old one.

A lot of companies have their own private brands in Japan, with one being the zany, buy-anything-and-everything-in-one-place retail chain Don Quijote.

Called Jonetsu Kakaku (literally “Passion Price”), this range of goods focuses on fun goods that are affordable and convenient to use, with one of its key features being customer feedback. The products are largely developed, and improved, by taking the opinions, requests and criticisms from customers into account, and one product recently getting a makeover is the battery-operated Ear Cleaner.

Our reporter Takashi Harada stumbled upon the new-and-improved ear cleaner during a recent visit to Don Quijote, or “Donki” as it’s affectionately known. Having purchased the original version a couple of years back, he was immediately drawn to the product, and when he saw the message “We responded to the genuine voice of customers!” on the package, he knew he had to try it.

▼ “We responded to the genuine voice of customers!”

The “voice of customers” wasn’t entirely glowing, apparently, as the original version received a fair amount of criticism from customers, who expressed the view that the suction power was just “so-so”. With some people saying cotton swabs removed more earwax, Don Quijote went into improvement mode, working to release this new product, which is said to have 25-percent more suction power.

Takashi was keen to find out if the new version really was an improvement on the original product, and because he had the original at home, he thought it would be the perfect opportunity to compare the two. So he picked up the Ear Cleaner 2 and took it home for a trial run.

▼ He still had the old box too, seen here on the left.

Starting with the price, the original cost 1,408 yen (US$9), and although Takashi assumed the new version would be more expensive due to the passage of time, he was surprised to find it was cheaper, at 1,099 yen.

It’s not every day that you find an improved product that’s cheaper than the original, but it seemed very in line with the nature of the range, which is known for delivering surprises.

▼ Taking a look at them in their cases, he could see that nothing looked too different on the surface, with all the parts being the same.

When he took them out of their boxes, they looked identical, with the only noticeable difference being the nozzle, which seemed harder on the new model, although that could’ve been because it wasn’t two years old like Takashi’s original cleaner.

▼ Original on the left, new version on the right

The only thing to do now was to compare the suction power. In order to do that, he refrained from cleaning his ears for about two weeks, and when he took both cleaners out and switched them on, he could hear that the new version clearly made a stronger whirring sound.

Putting one into each ear at the same time, he could feel that the new model had more force and seemed to have genuinely been improved, with noticeably more suction power.

However, when it came to removing earwax, Takashi says the original managed to remove more. He thinks this could be down to the different amount of wax he had in each ear, though, because he says the new version definitely felt like it had stronger suction power.

So will he be using the new model from now on? Well, he’s not entirely sure. He likes the familiar feel of the original, so he thinks he’ll keep going with that one for the time being, switching things up occasionally, but he reckons you won’t be disappointed with the new model. Whichever one you use, though, Takashi recommends using them with a dry ear for best results, and like anything you stick into your ear, it’s best to use with caution.

For Takashi, these battery-operated models are more enjoyable that picking your ears with a cotton swab, but it does take a bit of getting used to. Either way, it’s nice to know that Donki is listening to customers and actively responding to their requests with new and ever-more interesting products, which is part of the reason why their instant TKG egg sauces are so popular.

title: Roaming rubbish bin robot at Shinjuku Station solves the problem of where to put your trash
description: Japanese railway company comes up with a cute solution to one of the biggest problems for overseas tourists. As much as Japan is all about convenience and the spirit of hospitality, one thing that continues to confound visitors to Japan is the lack of trash cans. This can be particularly frustrating when you’re travelling and […]
content:
Japanese railway company comes up with a cute solution to one of the biggest problems for overseas tourists.

As much as Japan is all about convenience and the spirit of hospitality, one thing that continues to confound visitors to Japan is the lack of trash cans. This can be particularly frustrating when you’re travelling and enjoying the sights, because one piece of trash can quickly accumulate when you have no way to properly get rid of it.

It’s a problem that has long affected tourists as they eat and drink their way around all the different neighbourhoods, but now East Japan Railway (JR East) is coming to the rescue with a uniquely Japanese solution that not just solves the problem but is also fun to use.

The answer comes in the form of a rubbish bin that comes to you. Though that might sound crazy, it really is what the company is proposing, as it will be literally rolling out several mobile rubbish bin robots inside Shinjuku Station.

Each robot is designed to look like a train, with wide eyes on the front to attract the attention of passersby, and small nods to Shinjukuma, JR Shinjuku Station’s bear character, on the wrap.

The robot will automatically travel around the underground concourse on the first basement level – inside the East, West, Central East and Central West ticket gates – with openings on its sides for people to discard rubbish into as it passes by.

▼ The circular route.

The robot itself is an autonomous delivery robot capable of travelling both indoors and outdoors, developed by U.S. company Cartken and operated by Melco Mobility Solutions and Mitsubishi Electric.

JR East says the trial aims to improve service quality at stations while also making cleaning work more efficient, but the bigger question being addressed is whether a robot can actually navigate the crowds inside Shinjuku Station, which is often likened to a video game dungeon due to its expansive, labyrinthine layout.

The trial will examine how safely the robot can travel using its sensors and other onboard technology, as well as what problems arise when the station gets crowded. JR East will also look at whether the robot affects the movement of passengers through the concourse and how readily people accept the idea of having a mobile rubbish bin robot operating inside the station.

Shinjuku Station is known for being the busiest railway station in the world, so JR East is jumping into the deep end with the robot by trialling it under the most congested conditions. If the robot gets the green light after navigating this type of environment, we may see these little characters roaming around more stations in Japan in future.

For now, the trial is scheduled to take place on weekdays between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m., from 8 September to 20 November inside Shinjuku Station’s first-floor basement concourse. So if you have plans that will take you through the station during your travels, it might be worth holding onto your rubbish in the hopes of a robot encounter.

title: Eel sauce is our new favorite cooking hack for making any dish sweet and savory with zero hassle
description: Here are five app-eel-ing side dishes, rice bowls, and sweets for using up your leftover eel sauce. Unagi no tare (うなぎのたれ), literally “eel sauce,” has become our favorite all-around sauce. While the product may or may not contain small amounts of eel extract itself, it’s intended to be a perfectly thick, glossy accompaniment for grilled […]
content:
Here are five app-eel-ing side dishes, rice bowls, and sweets for using up your leftover eel sauce.

Unagi no tare (うなぎのたれ), literally “eel sauce,” has become our favorite all-around sauce. While the product may or may not contain small amounts of eel extract itself, it’s intended to be a perfectly thick, glossy accompaniment for grilled eel made from a simmered blend of soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar. Many commercially prepared versions exist, such as the one from Japanese brand Nihon Shokken, pictured below.

▼ Nihon Shokken’s eel sauce

This particular one does contain a tiny amount of eel extract but it’s not one of the top three ingredients. From the top those are soy sauce, mizuame (a Japanese sweetener), high-fructose corn syrup, and mirin, all ahead of the extract.

It was one of these bottles that we had purchased for use in one recipe but ended up having a decent amount of leftover sauce. Not wanting to waste it, we began experimenting with what we could use it on besides eel. It turns out that the sky is the limit when it comes to eel sauce’s potential–here are five ways to add it to easy Japanese homestyle dishes and snacks.

1. Grilled onigiri (rice balls)

First up is an easy and satisfying snack. Simply mix the eel sauce into the rice before shapjng the onigiri. We also threw in some leftover green onions and roasted sesame seeds for extra flavor.

Grill the onigiri in a pan or air fryer until you start to see faint scorch marks on the rice. The resulting snack has a deeper and richer taste than if using soy sauce alone.

2. Oyakodon (chicken and egg rice bowl)

Oyakodon is a hearty and delicious homestyle meal packed with protein and flavor. Begin by boiling the eel sauce with some water before adding chunks of chicken and onions. Let simmer until mostly cooked, then add in the beaten egg. Lay the mixture over a bed of rice to complete the dish.

The resulting eel sauce version was amazing, and involved less hassle than measuring out the individual ingredients for the simmering stock alone. We may always just use eel sauce from here on out.

3. Japanese amberjack

We actually picked this recipe up from food company Yamada Suisan’s YouTube channel. Grill the fish in a pan for a bit before adding equal amounts of eel sauce and water. Let simmer until the liquid is reduced.

It was an extremely simple dish involving hardly any prep. The cooked appearance was shiny and enticing, and while we enjoyed it very much, we also wished there was just a tiny bit more added sweetness. We’ll just make a mental note for next time.

4. Hard-boiled eggs

If you’re looking for a way to liven up your eggs, this is an easy hack for doing so. Let hard-boiled eggs with the shells removed soak in a closed bag with some eel sauce for about half a day. The resulting salty-sweet edge it provides is a perfect accompaniment for the eggs.

5. Mitarashi dango (glazed rice dumplings, usually skewered)

Add a small amount of water to some eel sauce in a pan and turn on the heat. We also added a tiny bit of potato starch to thicken it. When the sauce becomes viscous, add in some boiled-then-chilled shiratama dango (rice flour dumplings).

A quick taste test of the resulting mitarashi dango led us to add some kuromitsu (brown sugar syrup) to enhance the sweetness. That seemed to do the trick, so we recommend adding nearly equal amounts of eel sauce and either kuromitsu or sugar to make for a sweetly tantalizing dessert.

There you have it–five simple dishes to make using your leftover eel sauce. In fact, you probably wouldn’t even know they contained eel sauce if no one told you, since the overall ingredients are commonly represented in a variety of Japanese simmered and teriyaki dishes. Nihon Shokken’s eel sauce did leave us personally wanting to add a bit more sugar to the dishes at times, but this may not be the case with other brands or based on personal preferences.

We love finding novel ways to turn leftover ingredients into yummy new creations. Here are some of our top picks, from the weird to the wonderful.

title: New Shinkansen platform vending machine sells local-flavor treats from 127-year-old snack maker
description: A new way to get your hands on a popular souvenir at Shin Osaka. There’s a good chance you’re in a hurry if you’re about to hop on the Shinkansen. content:
A new way to get your hands on a popular souvenir at Shin Osaka.

There’s a good chance you’re in a hurry if you’re about to hop on the Shinkansen. After all, the bullet train network is generally the fastest option for long-distance travel in Japan, often even quicker than flying since it doesn’t require a time-consuming side trip to an out-of-the-way airport or lengthy check-in process.

And if you’ve got a full schedule of places to go and things to see, speedy snack procurement is also important, so now there’s a special Shinkansen platform vending machine in Osaka offering a popular local-flavor snack.

This bright yellow box at Shin Osaka Station is stocked with Osaka Ikaten, and for the uninitiated bears the in-English explanation that they’re “sea squid cradcker[s].” That might seem redundant, considering the lack of land squid in our world, but the “sea” part is probably included because these snacks are made by Bunkaku Sohonpo, a maker of seafood senbei (rice crackers) that’s been in business since 1899.

▼ Osaka Ikaten

Bunkaku Sohonpo is best known for their flagship Yukari brand of shrimp crackers, and shrimp are among the ingredients for Osaka Ikaten. The main draw here, though, is squid (ika in Japanese), which is accompanied by shiso (Japanese basil). Fans say the combination makes Osaka Ikaten deliciously flavorful, but without any harsh acridity that would give your taste buds mixed feelings about the eating experience.

Bunkaku Sohonpo is actually based in Nagoya, but when fans of their snacks in Osaka began asking for a special version, the company looked to Osaka’s food culture for inspiration. As a city of unabashed hearty eaters, Osaka has a number of foods it’s associated with, but ikayaki was the one that Bunkaku Sohonpo felt it could best honor with its particular kind of expertise. While in most parts of the country ikayaki simply refers to grilled squid, often served sliced and skewered, Osaka ikayaki is a little different, looking more like a folded squid dumpling or pancake.

Since its debut 11 years ago, Bunkaku Sohonpo’s Osaka Ikaten has become a popular souvenir among travelers in Osaka, and the Shin Osaka Station vending machine, which went into service last month, makes it even easier to pick up a pack either as soon as you arrive in the city or right before you leave. The machine is located on the platform shared by Lines 25 and 26, near where Car 9 of the Shinkansen trains stop, and offers a 12-pack of Osaka Ikaten for 950 yen (US$6) (cashless payment only). And if you’re looking for more unique vending machines in the same station, there’s another one just one platform over.

title: New Gundam megastore announced for one of Tokyo’s most popular tourist neighborhoods
description: A new mecha mecca is coming to Shibuya. The most famous landmarks in Shibuya have long been the statue of faithful dog Hachiko and the gigantic Shibuya Scramble crosswalk. But the downtown Tokyo neighborhood is a place where there’s always space for new trends, and recently there’s another must-visit spot for many travelers. The Shibuya […]
content:
A new mecha mecca is coming to Shibuya.

The most famous landmarks in Shibuya have long been the statue of faithful dog Hachiko and the gigantic Shibuya Scramble crosswalk. But the downtown Tokyo neighborhood is a place where there’s always space for new trends, and recently there’s another must-visit spot for many travelers. The Shibuya Parco shopping center has been establishing itself as a premier destination for Japanese pop culture fans, and that reputation is only going to grow when later this fall Shibuya Parco becomes the location of Japan’s newest Gundam specialty store.

The Gundam Base is a megastore chain dedicated to the Mobile Suit Gundam anime franchise. The main draw is a gigantic selection of Gunpla/Gundam plastic models, but they’re stocked with all sorts of other merch and collectibles too. With the Gundam franchise as a whole now spanning almost 50 years and over a dozen anime series set in multiple continuities, it can be hard for fans to find the specific items they’re looking for at smaller retailers, making a large-scale Gundam Base really feel like a supportive stronghold for fandom operations.

▼ Video of some of the existing Gundam Base stores

The announcement of The Gundam Base Shibuya comes less than two weeks after the start of the dismantling process for Tokyo’s life-size Gundam statue, which had its farewell ceremony on August 31. The 1:1-scale Unicorn Gundam stood in the Odaiba neighborhood, outside the Diver City shopping center. Diver City has a Gundam Base store of its own, called The Gundam Base Tokyo, and it appears that the Shibuya store will be operating in conjunction with it, not as a replacement. However, Odaiba is part of an island in Tokyo Bay, making it out of the way for many tourists’ itineraries, and with the loss of the Gundam statue leaving the neighborhood without one of its biggest attractions, Gundam rights-holder Bandai might be predicting a drop-off in customer traffic at the Odaiba store, making a location closer to the city center, like Shibuya, desirable.

The Gundam Base Shibuya will be located on Shibuya Parco’s 5th floor, which is designated as the “Chaos Culture Geek” section of the complex. Among its floormates will be Evangelion and Doraemon specialty shops, and one floor above it will be the Nintendo Tokyo and Pokémon Center Shibuya megastores, plus Capcom, Sega, Godzilla, Jojo’s Bizarre Adventure, and Weekly Shonen Jump shops, further cementing Shibuya Parco as a prime shopping spot for fans of otaku culture.

The Gundam Base Shibuya is scheduled to open in November of this year.

title: Studio Ghibli releases new onigiri rice ball-shaped lunch bag for Kiki’s Delivery Service fans
description: Carry your lunch like a magical delivery from the famous anime movie.  If you love Studio Ghibli as much as you love onigiri rice balls, then you’ll be happy to know that the studio is here to deliver, with a brand new lunch bag shaped like an onigiri, that fits two triangular convenience store rice […]
content:
Carry your lunch like a magical delivery from the famous anime movie. 

If you love Studio Ghibli as much as you love onigiri rice balls, then you’ll be happy to know that the studio is here to deliver, with a brand new lunch bag shaped like an onigiri, that fits two triangular convenience store rice balls inside.

Called the Insulated Rice Ball Shaped Lunch Bag, this sweet zippered pouch comes with a handle and a design that resembles a picnic basket, and is adorned with characters and motifs from the 1989 film Kiki’s Delivery Service.

▼ The lunch bag retails for 1,100 yen (US$7.12).

The beautiful triangular shape gives the pouch a unique look that makes it feels like it could be a package that Kiki might deliver by broomstick.

Although convenience store onigiri is given as the benchmark for what it can hold, the bag can comfortably fit small cut sandwiches, fruit, or if you’re feeling creative, one very large rice ball.

While Kiki appears on the front of the bag with Jiji, Jiji’s footprints appear on the back, alongside the title of the movie.

With aluminum-coated material on the inside, the bag has excellent cooling and heat retention properties, and the sturdy core material prevents the rice ball from getting crushed, which is another nice feature.

While the bag can be used for all sorts of things, the retail chain that sells it recommends using it as part of a wider picnic set dedicated to Kiki’s Delivery Service.

▼ Insulated Lunch Set – Medium (3,960 yen)

This handy set comes with two separate containers, a removable insulated tray and an ice pack, which can be popped into the mesh pocket to keep things cool.

▼ Insulated Lunch Set – Large (5,280 yen)

This larger version also comes with an ice pack and a removable insulated tray, but it includes four separate containers, with one divider for a large container and one for a small.

▼ Four-piece Plate Set (1,870 yen)

These gorgeous plates showcase two designs, one showing Kiki riding a broomstick, alongside Tombo riding a bicycle, with images of airships and clock towers evoking the town of Koriko. Jiji and his girlfriend Lily appear on the second design, with motifs that recall the bakery from the film.

▼ Stackable Cups with Container (1,650 yen)

No picnic is complete without drinks, and for that we have a four-piece cup set, with designs that match the plates.

The cups stack away neatly into the container, with a handle for easy transport and storage.

▼ Leisure Sheet – Medium (3,630 yen)

While people overseas might use picnic rugs on their outings, here in Japan people opt for “leisure sheets”, which are lightweight, foldable and water resistant.

▼ This one comes with an aluminium coating on the underside to protect against moisture and coldness.

Measuring 141 x 90 centimetres (55.5 × 35.4 inches), the leisure sheet folds up beautifully and is secured with a press-button closure.

▼ Leisure Sheet – Large (5,830 yen)

Whereas the smaller version featured Jiji and Lily with bakery motifs, this larger version is adorned with images of Kiki and Tombo in their town setting.

▼ The sheet measures 180 x 141 centimetres, and also folds up neatly and easily.

These products are perfectly timed for picnics now that the summer weather has eased up, making the days more comfortable for outdoor events. They can be purchased now at Donguri Kyowakoku stores and online (links below) while stocks last.

title: Ghibli’s Toshio Suzuki not impressed by generative AI images, Hayao Miyazaki thinks even less of them
description: As usual, Miyazaki doesn’t have time for anything that runs counter to his artistic principles. Almost as soon as generative AI image-making applications became something that the public had easy access to, “Ghibli-style AI illustrations” started getting shoveled into online spaces. Longtime fans of Ghibli that appreciate the studio’s human ethos in making art ground […]
content:
As usual, Miyazaki doesn’t have time for anything that runs counter to his artistic principles.

Almost as soon as generative AI image-making applications became something that the public had easy access to, “Ghibli-style AI illustrations” started getting shoveled into online spaces. Longtime fans of Ghibli that appreciate the studio’s human ethos in making art ground their teeth in frustration, while unconcerned technophiles were happy to have a way to avoid the thought and effort involved in the creative process and skip right to having a free facsimile of the basest elements of Ghibli aesthetics.

Studio Ghibli itself was pretty quiet on the whole subject, but company cofounder and longtime anime film producer Toshio Suzuki recently shared his thoughts on the use of AI to copy the Ghibli art style, and, in a sense, also shared how fellow Ghibli co-founder and director Hayao Miyazaki feels about it.

“When [Ghibli-style AI images] first started showing up online, I got asked about it a lot,” says Suzuki. “But I figured everyone would get tired of them pretty quickly. Sure enough, that’s what’s happened.”

Whether the loss of interest is quite as universal as Suzuki says could be debated, but postings of Ghibli-style AI images do seem to grab less attention these days. The ability of AI to generate images is no longer a novelty in and of itself, the obvious aping of the Ghibli house style rubs many of the more passionate fans of the studio the wrong way. But with AI capabilities continuing to advance, is Suzuki worried about it being used to create not just still images, but animation as well?

Not particularly. “AI can create certain types of animation, but people with a moderate amount of intelligence can see right through it. There’s not really much point to it. It’s not interesting or compelling.”

OK, so Suzuki clearly isn’t impressed or worried about generative AI. How, though, does Miyazaki, someone equally famous for his creative and curmudgeonly sensitivities, feel? Suzuki says “Miya-san doesn’t know what generative AI is in the first place.”

That might be a bit of a hyperbole on Suzuki’s part. At the very least, from a linguistic standpoint, “generative AI” is pretty straightforward, and despite his luddite leanings, Miyazaki must at least be aware that computers can now be used to generate images, so Suzuki’s comment might be a tongue-in-cheek way of saying that the director has such little interest in generative AI that he has no knowledge of it beyond the basic concept. Whether Suzuki is speaking literally or not, though, it’s clear that Miyazaki, as is so often the case, doesn’t really care what the rest of the industry is doing, and is as committed as ever to making his art his way.

It’s worth taking into consideration that Studio Ghibli, and Miyazaki in particular, enjoy a very unique position within the anime industry, and the entertainment industry as a whole, for that matter. Their unparalleled consistency in creating movies that are both critical and commercial successes mean that Ghibli can take all the time it wants to make its anime, and the involvement of Miyazaki is likely the only collateral needed to secure financial backing. Ghibli’s track record and prestige also mean that it can attract Japan’s top animator talent whenever it needs to gear up for a new project. Studios and directors whose resumes aren’t filled with modern classics, on the other hand, probably feel much more intense deadline and budget pressures, and thus stronger temptations from the presumed cost and time savings of AI, even if artistic quality suffers as a result.

Ghibli, though, has the option to quietly ignore generative AI, and Suzuki says that even if it becomes more prevalent in the industry, Ghibli will still be there as an example of the cultural value that can only come from human-made art.

Source: Mainichi Shimbun via Yahoo! Japan News

content:
Studio Ghibli specialty shop wants to keep your papercraft Totoro safe.

Studio Ghibli specialty shop Donguri Kyowakoku is packed with cute, beautiful, and otherwise awesome memorabilia from the anime production house’s animated films, from finger puppets to fountain figurines. If you’re looking for a lovely piece of art not only to display, but also to assemble yourself, the Paper Theater series is a perfect choice.

Each kit is composed of an array of wooden or paper pieces to cut out which form the characters and environment. The way in which the elements are layered creates a three-dimensional field of dept, creating a sense that you could step right into this little Ghibli pocket world, or maybe that its citizens could come leaping out into ours.

However, there’s also a downside to the Paper Theater series. They’re too thick to fit into the sort of frame you’d use for a poster, but they’re also not as sturdy or stable as a diorama-style figurine made of more substantial materials would be.

It’s bad enough if your anime art gets damaged, but it’s even worse when it’s something you put together yourself. Thankfully, Donguri Kyowakoku has just added specialized frames for displaying and protecting assembled Paper Theater projects to its inventory.

The frames are manufactured by Ensky, the same company that produces the Paper Theater kits. Two sizes are on offer, one which accommodates kits measuring 16 x 10 x 4.2 centimeters (6.3 x 3.9 x 1.7 inches), and the other kits with dimensions of 10 x 8 x 4.2 centimeters.

Those two sizes cover the vast majority of Ghibli Paper Theater sets, and each of the frames allows for either vertical or horizontal display, to match the orientation of the kit you’ve put together.

▼ The plastic frames have a wood-grain look to them and are available in “natural,” “pearl white,” or “ash brown” colors.

The small frames are priced at 2,200 yen (US$14) and the large ones at 2,750, while the Paper Theater kits themselves range from roughly 2,000 to 3,000 yen, with all of them offered through the Donguri Kyowakoku online store here.

content:
A new way to get a taste of Starbucks.

Starbucks has been working hand-in-hand with beverage giant Suntory in Japan, creating a number of canned and bottled beverages so even more customers can enjoy their drinks without walking into a branch.

Now, it’s going to be even easier to get a taste of Starbucks in Japan, as the chain has just announced it will be rolling out vending machines dedicated to their drinks, with each one adorned in Starbucks’ distinctive branding. The designs are based around the brand’s familiar green and black colour scheme, with a large Siren logo on the side, and the message “Anytime, anywhere, with ease, Starbucks” on the front in Japanese.

▼ The message will be accompanied by photographs of the drinks, being enjoyed in different settings.

The vending machines will be stocked with four Starbucks coffee drinks, two in cans and two in bottles, including an exclusive product that can only be purchased at the machine.

▼ One of the standouts is Coffee Signatures Black, a canned coffee that isn’t even out yet, as it will be released on 15 September.

This beverage is a first for Starbucks’ ready-to-drink coffee range in Japan, as it’s the only one to use espresso-roasted beans, giving it a rich aroma and full-bodied flavour.

▼ Another drink being released on 15 September is a revamped version of Starbucks’ My Retreat Caramel Macchiato,

This is the chain’s vending-machine-exclusive drink, featuring a combination of Starbucks coffee, milk and sweet caramel flavour.

▼ The other two drinks are the My Coffee Time Black…

▼ … and the My Coffee Time Cafe Latte.

Both these canned coffees have been on the market since November last year, and have been well received by customers. The Black version uses specially selected Arabica beans and is designed to have a fragrant coffee flavour without any excessive bitterness or astringency. The Cafe Latte combines dark-roasted coffee with milk for a richer, creamier taste.

▼ Nothing beats the fun, and novelty, of buying these drinks from a Starbucks vending machine.

Japan is home to many vending machines, and this newest addition to the landscape gives Starbucks lovers a fast and easy way to get their coffees. While the company is yet to reveal where they’ll be located, keep an eye for them in and around stations nationwide from mid-September.

title: Mt. Fuji may soon require off-season climbers to register with government or pay for their rescues
description: The question of whether it’s illegal to hike Mt. Fuji in the off-season is complex, and so is the question of who should pay for it. With this year’s Mt. Fuji climbing season now finished, forestry officials in Shizuoka, one of the two prefectures in which Japan’s tallest mountain has a footprint, are getting set […]
content:
The question of whether it’s illegal to hike Mt. Fuji in the off-season is complex, and so is the question of who should pay for it.

With this year’s Mt. Fuji climbing season now finished, forestry officials in Shizuoka, one of the two prefectures in which Japan’s tallest mountain has a footprint, are getting set for a meeting to analyze and evaluate things like the flow of hiking traffic on the trails and how well they were managed. They’ll also be discussing something related to climbing Mt. Fuji outside of the hiking season, and their decisions could lead to changes requiring lost or injured hikers to pay for the cost of their own rescues.

To recap, Mt. Fuji has an officially designated hiking season. The exact dates vary by year and trail, but in general the hiking season runs from early July to early September. The question of whether or not climbing outside of the official season is illegal or not is somewhat complex. As posted on the Mt. Fuji Official Climbing Website, under Article 46 of the Road Act, all official trails leading to the summit of Mt. Fuji are closed and prohibited from use during the off-season, and those who violate the restriction can face penalties of up to six months in prison and a fine of 300,000 yen (US$1,890). This restriction is based on the trails’ status as prefectural roads, which places them under the jurisdiction of their respective prefectures and allows for local authorities to prohibit their use.

▼ “Hey man, what’re you in for?”
“I hiked the Yoshida trail in December.”

On the other hand, ascending Mt. Fuji outside the climbing season, in and of itself, does not appear to constitute a criminal act. It is, however, strongly discouraged, and for several reasons. Attempting to climb the mountains without utilizing the trails means taking more dangerous routes, and even if off-season climbers were to illegally use the trails, they’re not maintained to a safe extent during that part of the year. Weather patterns on Mt. Fuji are more severe and unpredictable during the off-season, and mountain huts, relief centers, and other support facilities are not staffed, since no one is supposed to be on the mountain then. Together, these factors not only make climbing Mt. Fuji in the off-season a much riskier endeavor, but also means that off-season rescue operations are more difficult and expose rescue workers to greater dangers.

Currently, the expense of rescue operations are all paid for by the prefectural government, which is another way of saying that they’re paid for by residents who pay taxes to the prefectural government. With an increasing number of off-season incidents coming as the economy is doing poorly and many Japanese families are feeling the pinch in their household budgets, there’s been increasing anger at overconfident off-season hikers getting a free ride home after ignoring the warnings to stay off Mt. Fuji. Under the current laws, though, the government can’t stick hikers with the bill for their own rescue, since that’s classified as a guaranteed government service for people in distress.

What they might be able to do, though, is institute penalty fees for hikers who have failed to perform prior responsibilities, and so Shizuoka Prefecture is considering creating a new regulation that would require individuals to file an off-season climbing declaration with the local government if they’re going to hike Mt. Fuji outside of the official season. Off-season hikers who do not file the declaration would then be in violation of their responsibilities, which would, theoretically, open up the possibility of charging them for the cost of their rescue or imposing other penalties even if they were not found on the prohibited trails.

As the plan is still at the conceptual phase, it’s not clear whether all declarations would be automatically accepted, or if the process to file them would be purposely expensive or inconvenient in order to act as further discouragement. The committee is also said to be planning to discuss other measures such as making off-season climbing, whether on the trails or not, illegal. Yamanashi, the other prefecture Mt. Fuji is part of, is also reportedly looking for ways in which it could impose fines on off-season hikers who require rescue services.

title: 7-Eleven Japan’s Ramen Machine is a viral hit, but there’s one glaring problem
description: Well, two if you take into account how rare they are to find.  7-Eleven has been forging ahead of the convenience store pack in recent years with its range of automated countertop machines, letting customers whip up their own freshly made coffee, tea and smoothies. While the chain’s drink machines are widely known, not many […]
content:
Well, two if you take into account how rare they are to find. 

7-Eleven has been forging ahead of the convenience store pack in recent years with its range of automated countertop machines, letting customers whip up their own freshly made coffee, tea and smoothies.

While the chain’s drink machines are widely known, not many people know that at some branches you can find special ramen machines, which use the same system of automation to turn frozen ramen into piping hot, ready-to-eat ramen, all in a matter of seconds.

Despite having gone viral when they were first introduced, with the chain’s original introductory video receiving over 7 million views, the machines remain a hidden gem, as they can only be found at 40 locations, all in Tokyo’s neighbouring Saitama Prefecture.

After trying the machines in December last year and again in May, we’ve been waiting for them to be rolled out at more locations, but alas, the number of stores offering them has remained unchanged, sitting at 40, all in Saitama.

▼ The ramen varieties have expanded, though, with Taiwanese Mazesoba and Beef Udon recently added to the range.

When our reporter P.K. Sanjun headed out to Saitama to try the noodles, he came across an inherent problem which he’d like to share, as he thinks it might be one of the reasons why the machines haven’t been installed nationwide.

▼ First, though, he picked out a tub of noodles from the freezer and paid for it at the counter.

Popping the noodles into the machine, he was happy to find that it was an intuitive process, as he just needed to press a button and wait for the machine to do its thing.

As he watched, he was instantly impressed by the speed of it all, because less than a minute after putting the frozen ramen into the machine, and watching the giant metal rod pierce through the plastic lid to whip it up…

▼ … a piping-hot bowl of ramen was ready.

Normally, frozen ramen takes around three minutes in a microwave, or about five minutes if heating it up on a stovetop. The fact that the ramen takes just around a minute to be ready is a big part of the machine’s appeal, but after he took it out of the machine, that’s when he realised the one glaring problem with it.

▼ “Where am I supposed to eat this ramen?”

Like most 7-Elevens, this one didn’t have an eat-in space, and one of the staff members sensed his unease, saying, “Sorry, we don’t have anywhere for you to sit! I guess everyone eats theirs in their cars?”

Well, if he’d driven here, in-car eating would definitely be a good option, but he’d come here by public transport, and to make matters worse, it was raining that day. With one hand occupied with the task of holding an umbrella and the other holding a bowl of seriously piping-hot ramen, the whole experience almost felt like some sort of punishment.

When he did get around to tasting it, he found himself feeling incredibly self-conscious as he had to slurp up his noodles while standing outside the store, in front of arriving cars and curious passersby.

▼ P.K.’s alfresco dining setting.

Despite the embarrassment, the ramen itself turned out to be very tasty – the noodles had a satisfyingly firm texture, and the broth was hot and flavourful. At around 700 yen (US$4.38), it wasn’t a bad deal, especially considering the fact that it takes a minute to make and is available 24 hours a day.

Still, at stores in major cities and busy downtown areas in particular, you’re likely to run into the “Where am I supposed to eat this ramen?” problem. So in that sense, perhaps the ramen machine is better suited to regional areas, where people are more likely to be travelling by car.

In any case, 7-Eleven’s ramen machines are still going strong in Saitama so there’s no signs of them disappearing yet. Here’s hoping they make their way into Tokyo soon, so city workers like P.K. can enjoy them in the office, rather than having to eat them outside on the street.

U.S. dining and Japanese architectural design come together at this eye-catching new location.

Burger King has carved out a unique niche for itself in Japan, doing things differently to its competitors with all-you-can-eat deals, unusual menu items, and a vibe that’s arguably more independent and adventurous.

That sense of bold free-spiritedness is currently on display at a recently opened store in Noda City, Chiba Prefecture. Described as unconventional, the new branch has been attracting a considerable amount of attention online due to the building it’s housed in, as it looks like a traditional Japanese building.

The first thing you’ll notice about this branch is the roof, which is tiled in a way that makes it look like a traditional Japanese house. Seeing the Burger King sign on a roof like this looks totally out of the norm, creating a unique blend of Japanese tradition and fast-food Americana not commonly seen in Japan.

To a local, this is a very odd combination, because on the rare occasion that you see a big-name chain set up home in a traditional building in Japan, like this Starbucks in Kyoto, the signage and branding is also subdued to match the old-fashioned landscape.

▼ There’s no dialling down the Burger King branding here, as the sign stands loud and proud on the roof, just as it would on a regular-looking storefront.

Stepping closer reveals even more unique details, with a beautiful metallic rain chain by the front doors.

These rain chains are usually only seen on traditional homes or shrine and temple buildings.

Stepping through the front doors, however, reveals a very modern interior that makes it clear you’re in a Burger King.

As it turns out, this building used to be home to Aozora, a tempura restaurant by sushi conveyor belt restaurant chain Sushiro. When the new Burger King took over, it redid the interior and kept the Japanese-style facade, creating a unique branch.

▼ Wood and brick panelling gives the inside a very Western look.

Despite being newly opened, this was already a popular branch, with a constant flow of people coming and going through the doors when we visited. While some were clearly interested in the facade, stopping to take photos as they made their way from their cars, others were more interested in the food, especially with steak specials on the menu.

We couldn’t stop by a Burger King without trying something, so we bypassed the steak and opted for something a little more in line with the traditional vibe of the building.

▼ A Teriyaki Whopper Set…plus a Whopper Cheese Jr. to keep the U.S. fusion blend going.

Burger King burgers are known for being hefty, so staff are happy to cut them in half if you request it.

▼ The Teriyaki Whopper was delicious, giving us the salty sweet flavours of Japan.

▼ While the Jr. gave us the meaty American burger taste we’d been craving.

▼ It was a delicious meal made even more delicious by the sweet fusion style of the building.

So next time you find yourself craving a side of Japan with your Burger King burger, this humble branch has you covered. It’s nice to see the chain keeping the beauty of a traditional Japanese-style building alive, and there are plenty of other beautiful restaurant buildings we’d be happy to see the chain take up residence in too.

content:
Can we demolish a four-kilo purin made with 32 eggs? 

Be careful what you wish for. That’s something we’ve often heard wise people say, but we’re not always wise, nor are we always good listeners. That’s what led us to a cafe in Tokyo’s upscale Omotesando district the other day, where we pulled up a chair and ordered the stuff of dreams: a four-kilo purin.

That’s 8.8 pounds if you’re going by the Imperial system, and if you’re wondering what purin is it’s Japanese pudding, made with custard and similar to a flan or creme caramel. It’s also our reporter Natsuki Gojo’s favourite dessert, so when she heard about the massive, big-eats version, she immediately raced out to try it.

It was only when she arrived at the cafe, called Sweet Check, when the reality of what she was about to do hit her, and although she’d invited a friend to join her, she was unsure about whether or not they would be able to finish the huge dessert.

Still, eating massive amounts of endless pudding had always been a dream of hers, so she was determined to give it her all. However, when staff brought over a tray that took up almost the entire table, with a huge mould on top of it, she began to feel her pulse quicken.

When the mould was gradually removed, her eyes widened as the dessert slowly revealed itself.

Then, when the mould was completely released, the caramel sauce came flooding out like a waterfall.

▼ She was now face-to-face with her dream giant pudding!!!

Staff told her that this sweet beast weighs around 4 kilos and is made using 32 eggs and two litres (68 ounces) of milk. Natsuki had never thought about what actually goes into her favourite dessert so she decided to block the mental image of eating two dozen eggs in one sitting, and dipped her spoon into the silky smooth pudding for a taste.

It was a beautifully firm pudding, and the first bite revealed the rich flavour of custard, just how she likes it.

The caramel sauce had quite a strong bitterness, which helped to balance out the sweetness, and it felt decadent to eat it directly from the tray with spoons.

▼ If you prefer a fancier presentation, it can also be cut into pieces for serving, but we recommend carving out chunks with your spoon.

Natsuki was thankful that it wasn’t overly sweet, so she could easily eat mouthful after delicious mouthful. As she continued eating, she noticed that things were particularly creamy and delicious near the base of the dessert, where there appeared to be a thin layer of something different.

After asking staff about it, they told her this layer formed naturally under the weight of the pudding, and although it happens with all purin, it was more noticeable here due to its massive size.

▼ You can see the layer here, in white.

Natsuki felt it was a privilege to taste this exquisite creaminess, seeing as it’s something you can’t really detect in a regular pudding, and it gave her extra encouragement to keep going. At this point, she began to feel confident that she and her friend might actually be able to eat nearly all of the pudding, but as they continued eating, they both gradually began to feel full.

In the end, they put down their spoons and admitted defeat, because after eating about a third of it, they were unable to go on. Realising that the bounds of her stomach couldn’t match the vast bounds of her love for purin, Natsuki began to feel slightly defeated at her efforts. However, staff told her not to worry, as they’d never even seen a group of four finish one – they said you’d probably need around six people to eat the whole thing.

Thankfully, the leftover pudding can be taken home, which came as a welcome relief to our purin-loving duo. They probably left more than three kilos behind, so the bags they left with were incredibly heavy.

▼ The purin can also be freezed, so Natsuki’s visit wasn’t in vain as she now gets to enjoy pudding at home for weeks to come.

If you’d like to test your own purin powers, you’ll need to make a reservation at least two days in advance, as the giant pudding takes six hours to bake and one day to chill and set. There’s also a limit on how many can be made each day, so you’ll want to make your reservation as soon as you’ve decided on the date you’d like to visit.

At 5,000 yen (US$32.55) it’s a very affordable deal, especially if you’re going with a group, and it’ll definitely be a dining experience to remember. Just be sure to come on an empty stomach, and be careful what you wish for!

title: Visiting Fukui can teach travelers how to make, and smash, Japanese kawara tiles [Photos]
description: Echizen Seramika shares the techniques for both as part of its cool factory tour. Factory tours are a fun sightseeing activity in Japan, and a lot of travelers like to pick out places that not only show you how their wares are made, but also give you a chance to sample them for yourself. content:
Echizen Seramika shares the techniques for both as part of its cool factory tour.

Factory tours are a fun sightseeing activity in Japan, and a lot of travelers like to pick out places that not only show you how their wares are made, but also give you a chance to sample them for yourself. Usually that means production centers for snack foods or beverages, but today it’s taking us to a place where we won’t be tasting what the company makes, but smashing it with our fists.

Echizen Seramika is located in Echizen, Fukui Prefecture. Though the Seramika part of their name comes from “ceramic,” their specialty isn’t fancy pottery, but traditional Japanese earthenware roof tiles, called kawara in Japanese.

Fukui gets heavy snow in winter and high humidity year-round, so homes in the prefecture need roof tiles that can stand up to both weight and wetness. This has been the case for generations, and at one point there were dozens of companies crafting Echizen kawara, as tiles made with local materials are called. There are now only two manufacturers left, so visiting Echizen Seramika is an opportunity to see the preservation of part of Japan’s regional cultural heritage.

Tours are available by prior reservation and begin with a video presentation introducing the basic production process, after which visitors are led into the facility to see it for themselves.

The first thing we were shown was the factory’s massive clay pile.

Picking up a handful, we gave it a squeeze, and the subtly moist earth clumped into a ball in our palm.

However, raw, unprocessed clay doesn’t make for the sturdiest ceramics. Instead of using it as is, Echizen Seramika combs through the clay to find and remove large rocks or other objects that could prevent the clay from being molded into something with a uniform consistency and compromise the tile’s strength.

Once the clay has been suitably prepared, it’s placed into molds and pressed into shape using this apparatus.

Next, the molded clay is given time to dry before a glaze is applied. Then all that’s left to do is fire it in the kiln. If you’ve ever taken a ceramics class at school or a local store, you might be imagining something that looks like a pretty big oven, but in Echizen Seramika’s case, their tunnel-shaped kiln is 61 meters (200 feet) long!

After spending 24 hours in the kiln being fired at 1,200 degrees Celsius (2,192 degrees Fahrenheit), the tiles are ready to be shipped to customers.

As you can probably guess, getting a kiln that big up to that temperature is no quick or simple task, so instead of doing it every day, Echizen Seramika plans things out so that it does one or two firing batches every month, so you might not be able to see it in action when you visit. What can be guaranteed, though, is that you’ll be able to smash some tiles with your fists.

Now, while there’s ordinarily an undeniable appeal to the idea of channeling your inner karate master and delivering some ceramic-splitting strikes, you might feel a little guilty after having just taken a look at the care and craftsmanship that goes into their production. Worry not, though, because for the tile-smashing part of the tour, Echizen Seramika uses factory seconds, tiles that have been judged not good enough to sell as building materials.

That, in turn, might have you feeling surprised at the supply of seconds the factory has, but this isn’t a result of shoddy workmanship. Instead, it’s Echizen Seramika’s extremely high quality standards that keep them from shipping every tile they produce. In fact, their factory seconds are still so strong that they’re difficult even for trained martial artists to break. Because of that, Echizen Seramika uses a diamond cutter to add an additional partial crack in the center of the factory seconds before visitors take a swing at them.

Unleashing her fists of fury/factory fun on this day was our Japanese-language reporter Natsuno Futon.

As part of her tour reservation, Natsuno had requested a five-tile course. She could have elected to hit them all at once, but after talking things over with the tour guide, she instead opted to start with two tiles and work her way up to three at once for the finale.

Okay, Natsuno, show us your strength!

Oh, wow, Echizen Seramika wasn’t kidding when it said its products were tough. After Natsuno’s first attempt, the tiles remained uncracked. Thankfully, the guide stepped in here with some advice. Rather than punch straight down with her knuckles, he advised her to keep her thumb facing upward and pound down with an overhead swing…

…and that did the trick!

Invigorated and emboldened, Natsuno waited for her remaining three tiles to be put in place…

…and then she put them in their place with her newly acquired tile-smashing skills.

As mentioned above, reservations are required for the factory tour. Technically, the tour itself is free, but there is a fee of 500 yen (US$3.15) per tile you want to smash.

Oh, and if you’d rather make Echizen ceramics than break them, Echizen Seramika also offers miniature tile-making workshops, which also include a factory tour, for 3,000 yen. Reservations for both can be made through travel website Jalan here.

title: Japan’s middle-aged fairy man character stole our reporter’s heart in a hot spring town
description: Atsuo fell in love with Atami, and Natsuno fell in love with Atsuo. A lot of sightseeing destinations in Japan have their own mascot character, and the town of Atami, in Shizuoka Prefecture, is no exception. content:
Atsuo fell in love with Atami, and Natsuno fell in love with Atsuo.

A lot of sightseeing destinations in Japan have their own mascot character, and the town of Atami, in Shizuoka Prefecture, is no exception. As a matter of fact, Atami’s mascot is ready to greet travelers even before they’ve exited Atami Station.

With Japan’s love of cute characters, cuddly animals and fashionable young ladies are the most common mascot motifs, and looking at the above photo panel, you might assume that the kimono-clad woman on the right is Atami’s illustrated tourism ambassador. In actuality, though, it’s the combover-sporting gentleman on the left who fills that role.

According to his backstory, Atsuo, the official spokescharacter for the Atami Hot Spring Hotel and Ryokan Association, was once a young salaryman. One day, his company took an employee trip to Atami, which is famous for its hot springs, delicious seafood, and traditional inns. Atsuo liked the town so much that even when his coworkers headed back to the office, he, just, stayed in Atami…and he’s been there ever since.

In the in-story decades since he arrived, Atsuo has matured into a middle-aged man, but his daily baths in Atami’s hot spring waters have kept his skin remarkably youthful and shiny, even as his hair has thinned. Dressed in a yukata robe of the kind provided by traditional inns for guests to slip into after getting out of the bath, he also sports a neatly trimmed mustache. Oh, and he’s somehow become a fairy while living in Atami too, as he has a pair of gossamer wings sprouting from his back.

Though he may not fit into the conventional mascot mold, Atsuo has been warmly embraced by locals and visitors alike, including our Japanese-language reporter Natsuno Futon, who encountered him for the first time on a recent family trip to Atami. He’s got the associated line of character goods you’d expect for a proper mascot character, sharing shelf space with such luminaries as Pikachu and Doraemon in souvenir shops.

Atsuo’s profile lists his hobbies as taking hot spring baths, showing people around Atami, and generally helping out tourists who need a hand. His laidback but thoughtful aura quickly charmed Natsuno and her elementary school-age daughters, and before heading home at the end of their trip, they picked up some Atsuo merch, selecting a plushie, stickers, and terrycloth bath turban.

Natsuno’s kids were especially excited about the stickers, since puffy ones like these are booming in popularity right now in Japan.

▼ Each one has a little message, like “Thank you,” “Sorry!”, “Hang in there,” or “Get well soon.”

Each time Natsuno spotted Atsuo around town, her fondness for the character grew and grew, and by the time she and her family were headed to the station to catch a Shinkansen bullet train home, they’d become dedicated fans.

Just how dedicated? In front of Atami Station they came across a QR code that you can scan to take AR pictures with Atsuo…

…and they ended up having so much fun that they missed the train they’d been planning to get on, and had to hop on the next one half an hour later.

To be honest, Natsuno isn’t usually the type of person who treats mascot characters like a member of her traveling party, but Atsuo had earned a spot as part of the group, so they toasted him on their ride home.

He may not be the typical mascot, but he’s now definitely one of her favorites.
